learningObjective: Distinguish peak (best-case) speedup from geometric-mean speedup and understand the scope-limits of reported paper numbers such as those in GSPMD.
stem: A colleague summarizes GSPMD as 'partitioning gives 2× speedup end-to-end', citing a peak result from one model in the paper. Which TWO statements about interpreting such paper speedups are correct?

options.text: Any speedup reported in a systems paper is a property of the technique alone and is independent of the baseline; comparing against an older framework version is equivalent to comparing against its current version.

A paper's 'peak' speedup is the best-case observation on one (workload, hardware) pair; the geometric-mean speedup across the paper's full workload suite is typically smaller, so summarizing the paper by the peak overstates typical benefits.

Reported speedups are conditioned on that paper's hardware, software stack, workload set and baseline; treating them as a general property of the technique that transfers to arbitrary settings requires additional justification.
Peak and geometric-mean speedup are the same metric computed differently and can be used interchangeably as long as the workload set is identical.

explanation: A: peak is by definition the max, typically strictly larger than the geomean summary across a suite; using peak as a general claim overstates. B: paper speedups are conditioned on hardware, software stack, workload and baseline; the paper's numbers require restatement of conditions when generalized. C confuses two distinct statistics. D ignores that baselines evolve — comparing against an outdated baseline is not the same as comparing against a current one.

optionExplanations.B: Correct: peak-vs-geomean semantics and the overstatement risk.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: paper numbers are conditioned on the paper's setup.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: peak and geomean are different summaries.

assumptions: The reader understands geometric mean as (∏ speedup_i)^(1/N).
The comparison is across a multi-workload benchmark suite.
nonImplications: Does not imply peak numbers are useless; they are useful for characterizing best case.
Does not imply a paper's technique fails outside its evaluated setup; it means quantitative claims must be re-supported.
